title: Warren Moon on the Throwback Jersey Era: "I Was Just Proud That I Was a Part of It"
htmlContent:
In the early 2000s, a funny thing happened to sports history. It stopped living only in record books and highlight reels and started showing up in music videos. Rappers traded in their designer labels for vintage Mitchell & Ness jerseys, and suddenly the names and numbers of athletes from decades past were back in heavy rotation. For the players who once wore those uniforms, the moment was more than a fashion trend. It was a reminder of the mark they left.

Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback Warren Moon reflected on that moment in a conversation with Brandon "Scoop B" Robinson for his #WORDWITHSCOOP series, and his answer said a lot about how he views the era he played in.

Robinson set the scene with a question many fans of that era can picture. Imagine flipping through channels and seeing your favorite artists rocking throwback jerseys on screen, or hearing about it from younger relatives who were catching every new video. Did that make a veteran like Moon feel young? And what were the people around him saying?

Moon's response went beyond the question of age.

"It wasn't so much that it made me feel young, it just made me feel like my era was a memorable era," he told Robinson.

That distinction matters. Feeling young is personal and fleeting. Feeling that your era was memorable is about legacy, about knowing the time you lived through left something lasting behind.

For Moon, the 1980s and 1990s were not simply the backdrop to his football career. They were, in his view, one of the best periods anyone could have lived through. He pointed first to the music, calling it the best, and noted that hip-hop was just getting started then and kept improving from there.

He also recalled the towering entertainers of the time, naming Michael Jackson and Prince as superstars who defined the culture.

"I just thought that era of time was a great time to be in," Moon said.

The throwback craze was a perfect example of that era circling back. Hip-hop artists embraced retro jerseys as a statement of taste and knowledge, wearing the colors of franchises and players that a younger audience may never have seen play live. In doing so, they turned sports memorabilia into streetwear and introduced a new generation to the icons who came before.

Moon saw the bigger picture in that revival.

"Then you see all the things going on now with the throwbacks—jerseys, throwback uniforms, Starter jackets, all those different things," he said. "They were all during my time, so I was just proud that I was a part of it."

What stands out in Moon's answer is the absence of wistfulness. He is not longing to go back. Instead, he expresses pride. The resurgence of throwback gear confirmed something he already believed: that the years he played through were special, and that people still wanted to connect with them.

That pride carries extra weight when it comes from Moon. His path to the Hall of Fame ran through the Canadian Football League, where he won multiple Grey Cups with Edmonton, before he became a star with the Houston Oilers and went on to become the first Black quarterback enshrined in Canton. His career was built on persistence, and seeing his era honored in popular culture served as another form of recognition.

The throwback jersey trend eventually cooled, but its impact lasted. Retro uniforms remain a fixture in professional sports, and vintage apparel continues to sell to fans who were not even born when those players took the field. The line between sports and music, blurred so memorably in those early 2000s videos, has only grown thinner.

For Warren Moon, the lesson is simple. The music, the entertainers, and the athletes of the '80s and '90s created something worth remembering. When a new generation reached back for those jerseys and jackets, it confirmed what he had felt all along. He was not just watching a great era unfold. He was part of it, and he is proud of that.
excerpt: Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback Warren Moon reflected on the early-2000s throwback jersey craze with Brandon "Scoop B" Robinson, saying the trend made him feel not younger, but proud that his era — defined by hip-hop, Michael Jackson, and Prince — was one worth remembering.
